The Sichel (Pelecus cultratus) is a pelagic cyprinid of the family Xenocyprididae, widely distributed across the Ponto-Caspian basin and introduced to several European water bodies. Field surveys of adult populations in the Volga delta have recorded individuals attaining a maximum fork length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], a size that distinguishes this species from its smaller-bodied cyprinid relatives. This ultimate length is typically associated with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 2774 grams [Wwi = 2774 grams], a robust body mass that reflects the Sichel's streamlined, herring-like morphology adapted for sustained pelagic swimming. In contrast, the onset of gonadal maturation occurs considerably earlier in the life cycle, with individuals reaching puberty at a fork length of approximately 30 centimeters [Lp = approximately 30 centimeters]. The body mass at this developmental milestone has been estimated at 315 grams [Wwp = 315 grams] based on length-weight regressions derived from large-scale ichthyological surveys. These size thresholds for maturation are considerably larger than those observed in many other European cyprinids, likely reflecting the Sichel's relatively fast growth trajectory and its r-selected life-history strategy within a highly seasonal floodplain environment.

Reproductive investment in Sichel is characterized by a relatively modest fecundity per spawning event, with females producing approximately 822 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 822 eggs per clutch]. This estimate, derived from volumetric counts of hydrated oocytes in gravid individuals sampled from the middle Volga region during the spring spawning run, reflects the species' batch-spawning behaviour. The high frequency of spawning events is a defining feature of this species; individual females may complete approximately 365 spawning events per year [F_R_i = approximately 365 spawning events per year] during the extended reproductive period, yielding a daily reproductive output of approximately 822 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 822 eggs per day]. This combination of moderate per-clutch fecundity and extremely high event frequency reflects the energetic demands of gonadal recrudescence and is constrained by the short growing season in its native habitat. It is worth noting that all these reproductive measurements were recorded at the thermal regime characteristic of the species' spawning grounds in late spring, where water temperatures stabilize at 15 °C [T = 15 °C].

The early life stages of Sichel are marked by a very small initial body size, reflecting the production of small, pelagic eggs. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae, emerging from demersal adhesive eggs with a mean diameter of 1.7 millimeters, possess a wet weight at birth of only 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams]. This minute size, several orders of magnitude smaller than the mass of a juvenile at metamorphosis, places the Sichel firmly among the most fecund, small-egg-producing cyprinids. The endotrophic period, during which the yolk-sac larva relies entirely on its endogenous reserves, is brief, typically lasting no more than a few days before the onset of exogenous feeding. During this phase, the prolarvae drift passively in the pelagic zone, their transparent bodies and minimal mass making them highly vulnerable to both starvation and predation. The rapid absorption of yolk nutrients is critical, as any delay in first feeding due to low zooplankton densities can quickly lead to mortality at the point of no return, a common bottleneck for pelagic teleost larvae in temperate rivers.

Longevity in Sichel has been assessed through otolith-based age validation studies of wild-caught specimens. These analyses indicate that the maximum recorded lifespan in the species is 11 years [am = 11 years], a duration that is moderate for a cyprinid of its body size but relatively long when compared to smaller-bodied, short-lived species within the same family at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Importantly, this estimate of 11 years is derived from populations inhabiting the Volga-Caspian region, where the mean annual water temperature is approximately 15 °C [T = 15 °C]; in warmer, more southerly reservoirs where growth rates are accelerated, maximum longevity may be somewhat reduced. The species exhibits a relatively slow senescence rate, with individuals maintaining reproductive capacity well into their eighth or ninth year before a gradual decline in fecundity becomes apparent. This life span, combined with iteroparous reproduction, allows Sichel to buffer against years of poor recruitment, a common feature of species inhabiting unpredictable floodplain environments where early life survival is highly variable.

The combination of a moderate lifespan and an extremely high spawning frequency places Sichel at the fast end of the life-history continuum among cyprinids, despite reaching a relatively large ultimate size. While the pubertal length of 30 centimeters [Lp = 30 centimeters] is attained early in the growth trajectory, the ultimate fork length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters] is reached only by a small fraction of individuals that survive to advanced ages. Ecologically, the production of minute offspring weighing only 0.0026 grams [Wwb = 0.0026 grams] at birth and the capacity for nearly continuous daily spawning during the reproductive season represent classic adaptations of a pelagic broadcast spawner exploiting productive but highly unstable floodplain environments, where high early mortality is offset by sustained and frequent reproductive effort throughout the adult phase.
